Chapter I
Power-sharing
Overview
With this chapter, we resume the tour of democracy that we started last 
year. We noted last year that in a democracy all power does not rest 
with any one organ of the government. An intelligent sharing of power 
among legislature, executive and judiciary is very important to the design 
of a democracy. In this and the next two chapters, we carry this idea of 
power-sharing forward. We start with two stories from Belgium and Sri 
Lanka. Both these stories are about how democracies handle demands for 
power-sharing. The stories yield some general conclusions about the need 
for power-sharing in democracy.  This allows us to discuss various forms 
of power-sharing that will be taken up in the following two chapters.

Chapter 2
Federalism
Overview
In the previous chapter, we noted that vertical division of power among 
different levels of government is one of the major forms of power-sharing 
in modern democracies. In this chapter, we focus on this form of power-
sharing. It is most commonly referred to as federalism. We begin by 
describing federalism in general terms. The rest of the chapter tries to 
understand the theory and practice of federalism in India. A discussion 
of the federal constitutional provisions is followed by an analysis of the 
policies and politics that has strengthened federalism in practice. Towards 
the end of the chapter, we turn to the local government, a new and third 
tier of Indian federalism.

User:
How can we define a marketing role in a early stage startup?
Kimi:
In an early-stage startup, the marketing role is a hybrid of strategy, research, and hands-on execution. It is less about “running campaigns” and more about discovering whether the market actually needs what you are building and, if so, how to reach that market efficiently. Below is a practical framework you can adopt.
Core Mission: Achieve product–market message fit
The first marketer’s north-star metric is to validate the problem, the audience, and the wording that makes people care. That means the role is closer to “Head of Experimentation” than “Head of Marketing Communications” .
Pre-launch responsibilities (0–6 months)
• Customer & market research – 10–15 customer interviews every two weeks, competitor tear-downs, and channel mapping (where do prospects hang out, how do they currently solve the problem) .
• Positioning & messaging – craft one-sentence value propositions for each early segment; build the first pitch decks and landing pages to test resonance .
• Brand basics – choose a name, tone, and visual identity that will not embarrass you later, but do not over-polish; the brand will evolve .
• Launch plan – define wait-list vs. beta vs. public launch tactics, timelines, and success metrics .
Post-launch responsibilities (6–18 months)
• Growth experiments – run small paid-ads tests, SEO content sprints, referral loops, and partnership campaigns; double-down on whichever channel yields the lowest CAC .
• Instrumentation – set up the first KPI dashboard (traffic, trial-to-paid, CAC, LTV) and review it weekly .
• Sales enablement – create the first battle cards, objection-handling sheets, and case studies that the founder can use in early deals .
• Iterative messaging – refine value props with every cohort of new users; archive what does not convert .
Team structure options
• Solo marketer (often a founder) – handles everything from interviews to Google Ads; outsource design and dev task

(often a founder) – handles everything from interviews to Google Ads; outsource design and dev tasks .
• First hire – a “full-stack” growth marketer who can research, write copy, and launch ads; fractional CMO for strategic oversight if budget allows .
• 2–10 employees – add one marketing generalist and a part-time content or paid-media freelancer .
Skills that matter most
• Structured interviewing & note-taking
• Rapid landing-page or no-code tooling
• Basic analytics (Google Analytics, Mixpanel)
• Copywriting that converts
• Comfort with ambiguity and weekly pivots
A concise job description you can post today
Title: Founding Growth Marketer
Mission: Find the message and channel that turn strangers into paying customers within 90 days.
Key tasks: customer interviews, positioning docs, launch experiments, KPI dashboard.
Must-haves: 2+ growth experiments shipped, fluent with GA4 or Mixpanel, excellent written English.
Nice-to-haves: early-stage startup experience, design eye, SQL.
By defining the role this way, you keep the focus on learning and traction rather than on polished-but-untested marketing activities.

Abstract Human Resource Management (HRM) is undergoing a structural shift driven by advances in artificial intelligence. Instead of isolated point solutions, organizations are assembling integrated, data-first HRM models that couple intelligent prediction with agentic execution, creating closed-loop systems that learn from outcomes. This essay explains the contours of that breakthrough. We define a modern HRM model, outline enabling AI capabilities, and connect them to value in talent acquisition, skills intelligence, learning, performance, workforce planning, engagement, HR service delivery, compliance, and governance. We then examine architecture patterns, data stewardship, fairness and privacy practices, adoption tactics, and a staged implementation roadmap. The argument is simple: HRM ceases to be a back-office function and becomes a strategic, continuously optimizing system of work, with people analytics, large language models, and autonomous agents acting as a nervous system for the enterprise. The result is better hiring, faster reskilling, more equitable decisions, and measurable business impact when models are designed responsibly.
Introduction For decades, HRM oscillated between administrative efficiency and strategic ambition. Transactional workloads—payroll, benefits, case management—consumed capacity, while “strategic HR” remained a slideware aspiration. AI changes the production function of HR. Language models elevate knowledge work; representation learning unlocks skill inference; forecasting tightens workforce planning; and agentic automation shortens the loop from insight to action. The breakthrough is not any single model, but an operating model that integrates data, models, and workflows around continuous learning. In this model, policies are executable, employee journeys are personalized at scale, and the organization moves from annual cycles to on-demand adaptation. Critically, success depends on guardrails: ethical use, transparency, and partic

-demand adaptation. Critically, success depends on guardrails: ethical use, transparency, and participatory change. This essay treats AI as an instrument, not a mystique, and shows the practical shape of a next-generation HRM model.
What We Mean by an HRM Model An HRM model is a structured description of how an organization attracts, develops, deploys, and retains talent to achieve outcomes. It specifies inputs (people data, business context), processes (hiring, learning, performance, mobility), controls (policies, compliance), and outputs (capability, engagement, productivity). In a traditional model, data is fragmented across systems of record; policies are documented but not executable; decisions rely on lagging indicators; and improvements are episodic. In an AI-enabled model, data is unified in a governed layer; policies are encoded as decision rules enriched by models; decisions use leading indicators; and improvements are continuous because outcomes feed back into learning objectives. The model is socio-technical: tools, processes, and behaviors co-evolve. It is also plural: organizations tailor the model to context (industry, regulation, labor markets, culture) while reusing common architectural patterns.
Why This Is a Breakthrough Now Four forces converge. First, language models enable machines to read, synthesize, and act on unstructured HR content—job descriptions, resumes, policies, survey verbatims—previously trapped in documents. Second, representation learning for skills turns job data into vectors, powering matching, mobility, and learning recommendations that understand similarity beyond keywords. Third, causal and time-series models, combined with simulation, improve workforce planning under uncertainty by testing policy scenarios before big bets. Fourth, agentic automation coordinates multi-step workflows across HR and business systems—scheduling interviews, drafting offers, triggering learning, or initiating mobility—closing the loop from predict

terviews, drafting offers, triggering learning, or initiating mobility—closing the loop from prediction to action. Cloud-native data platforms, cheaper compute, and maturing MLOps make this feasible for mid-sized firms, not only global enterprises. The limiting factor shifts from technology to governance and change.
Reference Architecture for an AI-Enabled HRM Model A pragmatic architecture has five layers. (1) Data foundation: a governed lakehouse with canonical entities—person, role, skill, competency, event, policy, and outcome—fed by HRIS, ATS, LMS, survey, collaboration, and business systems. PII is minimized, access is role-based, and purpose-specific views are provisioned. (2) Intelligence layer: a portfolio of models—entity resolution, skill extraction, matching, attrition and ramp-up models, performance predictors, scheduling optimizers, and LLMs for summarization and reasoning. (3) Orchestration and agents: task-oriented agents that plan, act, and verify across tools with human-in-the-loop checkpoints for material decisions. (4) Experience layer: manager and employee surfaces—copilots inside familiar tools and mobile experiences—that explain recommendations and support counterfactual exploration. (5) Governance: model registry, evaluation harnesses, audit trails, consent services, prompt and policy catalogs, and a Responsible AI board that sets standards and reviews releases. The goal is modularity: swap models without breaking flows, and keep humans empowered to supervise and override.
Talent Acquisition Reimagined Hiring quality is a compound function of reach, screening, assessment, candidate experience, and speed. AI improves each component. Intelligent sourcing expands reach by inferring adjacent skills and identifying non-obvious talent pools. Screening accelerates without crude filters: models cluster experience and projects rather than over-index on pedigree. Assessments become multimodal: work-sample generation, code critique, case summarization,

pedigree. Assessments become multimodal: work-sample generation, code critique, case summarization, and structured interviews scaffolded by LLM prompts raise signal while reducing bias through consistent rubrics. Candidate experience improves through responsive, transparent assistants that answer questions, schedule interviews, and provide constructive feedback. Time-to-offer drops because agents coordinate logistics in hours, not days. Governance matters: model explanations, adverse impact monitoring, opt-out pathways, and clear data retention windows protect candidates and the brand.
Skills Intelligence as the New Currency Job architectures are brittle when work changes faster than titles. Skills-centric representations are more granular and durable. AI extracts skills from resumes, projects, learning artifacts, and code repositories, then embeds them for matching and gap analysis. Managers use skills graphs to plan roles, design teams, and budget for capability building. Employees see personalized paths: “Given your current profile, here are three projects that will stretch you and the two courses most likely to close the gap.” Internal mobility accelerates because matching understands transferable capability, not just identical job codes. The breakthrough is feedback: as people complete projects and perform, models update skill vectors and confidence scores, improving recommendations over time. This shifts HR conversations from job ladders to capability portfolios, aligning talent supply with business demand dynamically.
Learning and Development at Personalization Scale Corporate learning historically fought the engagement paradox: employees want targeted, purposeful learning but were offered generic catalogs. LLMs help by curating micro-curricula from enterprise content and public sources, summarizing long videos or documents into role-relevant, 15-minute learning paths. Retrieval-augmented generation ties learning to company context. Spaced repetition, quizzes

g paths. Retrieval-augmented generation ties learning to company context. Spaced repetition, quizzes, and reflection prompts are tailored by performance data and upcoming work assignments, improving retention and transfer. Mentoring becomes programmatic: agents propose mentor-mentee matches, schedule sessions, and suggest talking points based on skills goals and recent work. Learning now sits inside the flow of work: a developer receives an inline code walkthrough; a sales rep gets a brief on a new product before a call; a manager is coached on feedback language minutes before a review. The metric shifts from course completions to performance lift and time-to-competence.
Performance, Goals, and Feedback Annual reviews compress a year of complexity into one brittle decision. AI supports continuous performance management by synthesizing evidence across artifacts: commits, tickets, documents, customer feedback, and peer notes—always with consent and scope. LLMs draft goal statements that meet SMART criteria and align with strategy. During cycles, assistants help managers frame evidence-based feedback, counteract recency bias, and calibrate ratings against rubrics. Employees receive coaching on self-reviews and prepare promotion cases with transparent evidence. Calibration sessions draw on anonymized distributions and simulated outcomes: “If we tighten criteria X, anticipated impact on group Y is Z.” None of this replaces judgment. Rather, it makes judgment more informed and equitable by surfacing signals and counterfactuals early and often.
Workforce Planning and Scheduling Strategic workforce planning blends macro supply, internal mobility, and productivity levers. AI brings scenario planning to the edges: planners simulate demand shocks, automation adoption, or regional policy changes, and see implications for hiring, reskilling, and redeployment. At the micro level, schedulers optimize shifts with fairness and preference constraints, reducing burnout and overtime. R

chedulers optimize shifts with fairness and preference constraints, reducing burnout and overtime. Ramp-up models estimate how quickly new hires reach proficiency given role complexity and supervisor capacity, thereby shaping recruiting and onboarding plans. When plans change, agents coordinate offers, transfers, and learning enrollments, reducing handoffs. The breakthrough is the integration of forecasting, optimization, and orchestration, so plans are executable rather than aspirational.
Employee Experience, Engagement, and Well-Being Engagement surveys surface themes, but action stalls when findings are vague. LLMs cluster open-ended feedback into precise, manager-level improvement opportunities and generate action ideas grounded in evidence: “Meeting load is the top drain for Team A; trial a no-meeting block and measure outcome Y.” Well-being programs personalizes nudges that respect boundaries—time-zone aware reminders, burnout risk alerts based on workload patterns, and proactive resource suggestions. Employees interact with a single, trustworthy assistant that knows benefits, policies, and learning pathways, and can escalate to humans smoothly. Transparency is crucial: employees see what data is used, with controls to opt out of sensitive signals. Trust multiplies impact; opacity kills it.
HR Operations and Policy Automation HR service desks are ripe for transformation. Policy bots answer most questions with grounded, company-specific reasoning and cite sources. Case triage classifies and routes issues with predicted effort and risk. Document generation—offers, contracts, amendments—moves from templates to parameterized blueprints with compliance checks. Onboarding checklists become orchestrations that verify completion and proactively remove blockers. Offboarding reverses symmetry with empathy: knowledge capture, alumni network invitations, and eligibility calculations are automated yet human in tone. The breakthrough is not deflection; it is first-contact r

culations are automated yet human in tone. The breakthrough is not deflection; it is first-contact resolution with clarity and empathy, freeing HR capacity for strategic work.
Compliance, Risk, and Governance Regulatory obligations—equal employment opportunity, data protection, labor standards—tighten as AI proliferates. Governance starts with data minimization and purpose limitation: collect only what is needed for stated outcomes, and separate identity from behavior wherever possible. Access controls enforce least privilege; audits verify that training and inference honor consent. Fairness is a process: define harm hypotheses; measure group disparities; remediate with feature constraints, threshold adjustments, or alternative objectives; and re-evaluate continuously. Documentation matters: model cards, decision logs, and policy catalogs enable internal and external scrutiny. Finally, set escalation thresholds: certain decisions—terminations, high-stakes compensation moves—remain human-led with AI as an advisor only. A strong governance spine enables bolder innovation.
Privacy, Security, and the Ethics of Visibility HR data is some of the most sensitive in the enterprise. AI systems must be private by design: encryption in transit and at rest, confidential computing for high-risk inference, data loss prevention in prompts and outputs, and red-teaming for prompt injection or data exfiltration. Differential privacy and aggregation protect individuals when reporting trends. Transparency dashboards show employees what profiles and inferences exist and allow corrections. Opt-in pilots demonstrate value before broader rollout. Ethics is not a poster; it is a set of daily choices—what to model, what to ignore, and when to slow down. The credibility of the HR function depends on getting this right.
Agentic Workflows and the Human in the Loop The leap from predictions to outcomes requires action. Agent frameworks structure multi-step HR tasks: plan (decompose goal), act (in

omes requires action. Agent frameworks structure multi-step HR tasks: plan (decompose goal), act (invoke tools and systems), and verify (check outputs against constraints). For example, an internal mobility agent might shortlist candidates, request manager approvals, schedule interviews, draft offers, update HRIS, and trigger onboarding—all with audit trails and stop points. Human oversight shifts from doing every step to supervising key junctions, investigating exceptions, and refining policies. This division of labor respects expertise while scaling impact. Importantly, agent goals must be bounded and reward functions aligned with human values to avoid Goodhart’s law in people systems.
Economics and ROI AI programs compete for capital. HR leaders should quantify value in three buckets: (1) direct efficiency—case resolution time, recruiting cycle time, recruiter and HRBP capacity released; (2) effectiveness—quality-of-hire, retention of pivotal roles, time-to-competence, quota attainment; and (3) risk reduction—lower compliance incidents, improved audit readiness, fewer bad decisions. Costs include data work, model development or procurement, platform fees, change management, and governance. Build a portfolio view: quick wins (policy bot, interview scheduling) fund foundations (skills graph, data lakehouse) that enable step-change value (internal mobility marketplace, agentic onboarding). Treat models as products with owners, roadmaps, SLAs, and post-release learning.
Case Vignettes Consider three sketches. A regional bank unifies ATS, HRIS, and learning data to build a skills graph. Within six months, internal fills rise for cyber and analytics roles because matching looks beyond titles. A manufacturing firm uses LLMs to capture tacit knowledge from retiring experts, turning tribal know-how into searchable, trainable assets. Ramp-up time in maintenance drops by weeks. A global retailer deploys a policy bot grounded in its handbook and collective agreements. First-

s. A global retailer deploys a policy bot grounded in its handbook and collective agreements. First-contact resolution climbs to 80 percent, and HRBP time shifts to strategic workforce planning for store openings. None of these require moonshots; they require focus, governance, and iteration.
Implementation Roadmap Start with intent. (1) Clarify business outcomes with executives: which roles, capabilities, or programs are most material in the next twelve months? (2) Map data realities: where do core entities live, who owns them, and what quality issues block progress? (3) Stand up a minimal platform: identity, storage, governance, model hosting, and an evaluation harness. (4) Pick one end-to-end journey—say, internal mobility—and instrument it. (5) Build or buy a skills extractor and a matching model; test fairness and accuracy with real stakeholders. (6) Integrate with ATS and HRIS for action, not just dashboards. (7) Launch a pilot with opt-in teams; publish results, lessons, and changes. (8) Establish a Responsible AI review that meets at defined milestones. (9) Expand to learning recommendations and interview orchestration; reuse the skills foundation. (10) Add observability: drift detection, performance by cohort, and human override logs. (11) Codify operating rhythms: weekly triage, monthly model review, quarterly roadmap. (12) Scale via enablement: documentation, templates, prompt libraries, and communities of practice so HRBPs and recruiters co-create, not just consume.
Operating Model and Roles Successful programs clarify ownership. HR owns problem definition, policies, change, and adoption. Data and AI teams own platforms, modeling standards, and guardrails. Product managers own outcomes for each journey (e.g., mobility, hiring). Legal, security, and ethics provide gatekeeping and guidance. A cross-functional design council reviews employee experience, with representation from diverse employee groups. New roles emerge: skills architect, HR agent designer,

representation from diverse employee groups. New roles emerge: skills architect, HR agent designer, fairness analyst, and policy engineer. Training evolves: HR professionals learn promptcraft, data literacy, and how to interpret model outputs; technologists learn employment law basics and change management. Collaboration shifts from ticket-based to product-based, with shared backlogs and metrics.
Change Management and Communication Technology adoption fails without trust. Explain the “why” in business terms, and the “how” in human terms. Demonstrate that AI augments, not replaces, HR professionals and managers. Invite employees into design through surveys, pilots, and open demos. Publish clear FAQs: what data is used, how recommendations are made, how to correct errors, and how to opt out when appropriate. Equip managers with talk tracks for team discussions. Celebrate early wins with concrete stories and numbers, not platitudes. Address concerns promptly; non-answers breed rumors. Change is a product: launch, learn, and iterate.
Interoperability and Vendor Strategy Most organizations will combine platforms and point solutions. Avoid lock-in by insisting on open standards for skills taxonomies, event schemas, and model interchange. Design for interchangeability: if a better extractor or matcher emerges, it should slot in without re-plumbing. Maintain a vendor scorecard that weighs capability, roadmap alignment, security posture, and pricing model. Balance buy and build: build where differentiation matters (skills graph tuned to strategy); buy where utility suffices (scheduling, transcription). Negotiate data rights explicitly so you can export embeddings and fine-tuned models if you switch providers.
Measuring Impact and Ensuring Fairness Define metrics before launch, not after. For hiring, track quality-of-hire proxies, cycle time, pass-through by cohort, and candidate satisfaction. For mobility, measure internal fill rate, time-to-role, and diversity of moves. For

te satisfaction. For mobility, measure internal fill rate, time-to-role, and diversity of moves. For learning, measure time-to-competence, assessed proficiency, and application on the job. For engagement, combine perception, behavior, and outcomes to avoid single-source bias. For fairness, evaluate parity of opportunity and error rates across groups, and publish results to governance forums. Use A/B or phased rollouts to attribute changes credibly. Treat fairness regressions as incidents with owners and SLAs, not as generic “we’ll look into it.”
Future Directions Three frontiers are emerging. First, work graphs replace org charts: instead of boxes and lines, we model tasks, dependencies, skills, and tools, enabling precise matching and dynamic team formation. Second, digital twins of the workforce let leaders simulate policy changes—hybrid schedules, pay bands, automation—and see effects on productivity and equity before implementation. Third, privacy-preserving learning (federated learning, synthetic data, secure enclaves) enables cross-company benchmarking and skill portability without exposing PII. As interfaces converge on natural language and multimodal input, employees will steer their careers by conversing with trustworthy copilots. The HR function that masters these frontiers becomes a strategic accelerator for the business, not a cost center to be optimized.
Conclusion The HRM model breakthrough in AI is not a gadget; it is a disciplined redesign of how talent systems sense, decide, and act. The ingredients are now within reach: a governed data foundation, a portfolio of well-evaluated models, agentic orchestration with human guardrails, and an adoption program that earns trust. When composed thoughtfully, these capabilities elevate hiring quality, speed reskilling, improve fairness, and make change an everyday competence. The prize is organizational agility powered by human potential. The work ahead is to build responsibly, measure honestly, and keep peopl
